title: AI-Powered Chatbots in Science Education: Meta-Analysis of Pedagogical Integration and Student Achievement
venue: International Journal of Chemistry Education Research
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-powered chatbots improve student achievement in science education and which factors explain variation in effectiveness. The authors note that prior work has often focused on technical features or user satisfaction rather than instructional design, learner context, or learning outcomes, so they conduct a moderator-rich meta-analysis to address these gaps.

The intervention studied is chatbot-supported instruction, including tools such as ChatGPT, virtual teaching assistants, and other AI-powered conversational systems. The review synthesized 26 empirical studies published from 2020 to 2024 using a random-effects meta-analytic model and moderator analyses. The included studies covered science-related subjects such as biology, physics, medical/health sciences, computer science, programming, and mathematics, across primary, secondary, and higher education contexts in multiple countries.

Overall, chatbot use had a moderate positive effect on achievement, but effects varied substantially by context and design. The strongest outcomes appeared in lower-middle-income countries, in scaffolded and personalized learning environments, with longer interventions and with assessments targeting higher-order thinking or mixed outcomes. The review concludes that chatbots are not uniformly effective and should be integrated as context-sensitive pedagogical supports rather than one-size-fits-all tools, especially given weaker or mixed effects in mathematics and health-related subjects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis following PRISMA with a random-effects model, explicit risk-of-bias assessment, heterogeneity analysis, and publication-bias checks. The paper synthesizes 26 empirical studies with quantitative effect sizes, meeting the highest evidence-quality standard in this framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect on achievement is moderate and clearly positive (g=0.610), exceeding the blue threshold for impact. The review also reports robust positive subgroup effects in several contexts, indicating meaningful practical impact rather than a trivial or ambiguous one.

interventions.use_case: AI-powered chatbots and conversational assistants (including ChatGPT-based tools) used for science education, often as scaffolded or personalized learning supports and sometimes as primary instructional agents.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-analysis found a statistically significant moderate positive effect of AI-powered chatbots on student achievement in science education, pooled Hedges’ g=0.610 (95% CI 0.550–0.670, p<0.001) across 26 studies (n=3,287). The outcome was science learning achievement, with stronger effects when chatbots were used in scaffolded or personalized science learning contexts.

Across the included studies, chatbots commonly improved engagement, motivation, and satisfaction. Moderator analyses showed positive effects on noncognitive outcomes such as satisfaction/perception (g=1.803) and engagement/motivation (g=0.761), though self-efficacy results were mixed.
finding.effect_size: g=0.761 to 1.803 (subgroup effects); overall noncognitive ES=0.801
finding.confidence_interval: Overall noncognitive 95% CI 0.424–1.178; subgroup CIs vary

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that chatbot-supported instruction had stronger effects on higher-order thinking and mixed HOTS/LOTS assessments than on lower-order measures. Moderator results were positive for HOTS (g=0.974) and especially mixed assessments (g=1.778), suggesting gains in critical thinking, problem-solving, and conceptual transfer.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills, critical thinking, problem-solving, conceptual understanding
